2.5.10 Illegal Activity Identification (VCS, 3.19; CCB, G5.4)

The Katingan Mentaya Project is situated in an area historically affected by illegal logging, mining, 
and the hunting of protected species, alongside unauthorised use of fire for land clearing. To 
combat these issues, the project has implemented a strategy that integrates advanced 
monitoring technology with community involvement. 
 
By using satellite imagery and drone surveillance, the project can monitor for signs of illegal 
activities across its expansive territory in real-time. This technological approach is supported by 
encouraging local communities to report any suspicious activities, effectively making them active 
participants in the conservation efforts. 
 
To address the root causes of these illegal activities, the project works on several fronts. It 
collaborates with local and national governments to strengthen laws against illegal resource 
extraction and ensure robust enforcement. Rapid response teams are established to respond 
quickly to any illegal activities, ensuring those caught are prosecuted. 
 
Education plays a critical role in the strategy. The project runs educational programmes for the 
local communities to emphasise the value of conservation and the adverse effects of illegal 
activities. These programmes aim to shift traditional views that lead to environmental 
degradation by showcasing the benefits of sustainable practices. 
 
The project also promotes sustainable livelihood options such as agroforestry, Climate Smart 
Agriculture, eco-tourism, and sustainable fishing. These initiatives offer economic alternatives to 
communities, reducing their reliance on illegal practices and enhancing their economic stability. 
 
A significant aspect of the project's approach involves clarifying and strengthening land tenure 
rights. By securing legal recognition of land ownership and use rights for the communities, the 
project decreases the likelihood of illegal exploitation. It supports the creation of community-
managed forests, where locals directly manage and protect their environment, fostering a sense 
of ownership and stewardship. 
 
To uphold ethical standards, the Katingan Mentaya Project has implemented strict policies 
against forced labor, child labor, and human trafficking. Regular audits ensure these policies are 
followed across all operations and supply chains. Additionally, the project ensures fair labor 
practices, including safe working conditions, fair wages, and the right to collective bargaining. 
 
The project maintains transparency in its operations, with frequent reporting on its efforts to 
combat illegal activities and uphold ethical labor practices. It engages with local communities, 
NGOs, and government agencies as partners in conservation, ensuring broad support and 
accountability. This engagement also includes addressing any community concerns about the 
project’s impacts on their lands and livelihoods.

Diversity within the Community  
 
Initially, social, economic, and cultural diversity within the community was relatively limited, with 
most households following similar subsistence-based economic activities and shared cultural 
practices. Economic diversity was limited, with wealth disparities present but not pronounced. 
Gender roles were traditional, with men more involved in public and economic decision-making, 
while women managed household finances and domestic affairs. Age-wise, the community was 
predominantly middle-aged, with young adults participating minimally in community leadership or 
conservation activities.  
 
Since the project's initiation, diversity within the community has evolved, particularly 
economically. Project’s programmes have facilitated diversification in livelihoods, with a shift 
from predominantly agricultural work to engagement in trade, formal employment, and service 
sectors. This shift has led to emerging wealth variations within the community as some 
households capitalise on new economic opportunities, while others remain engaged in traditional 
subsistence activities.  
 
Efforts to improve gender inclusivity have encouraged greater participation from women, 
especially in community meetings focused on health and environmental issues. While traditional 
gender roles persist, there is now a growing representation of women in community-led initiatives. 
Additionally, younger community members are increasingly involved in the project’s 
environmental programmes, showing greater intergenerational engagement in conservation 
practices.
4.1.2 Interactions between Communities and Community Groups (VCS, 3.19; CCB,

In our commitment to sustainable community engagement and the application of the 
precautionary principle, we have established measures to mitigate potential negative impacts on 
community well-being, particularly for vulnerable groups such as women, girls, children, and other 
marginalised populations, as well as for the maintenance and enhancement of high conservation 
value (HCV) attributes related to community well-being.  
 
Current and Future Measures for Community Well-being and Environmental Protection  
 
Participatory Planning and Consultation 
We have implemented a participatory planning process, central to which are ongoing 
consultations with community members. This approach facilitates the early identification and 
discussion of potential negative impacts, such as air and noise pollution, water discharges, waste 
generation, and the release of hazardous materials. By directly involving community members, 
especially representatives of vulnerable groups, we ensure that our project design addresses 
their unique needs and concerns (UNDP, 2018; IFC Performance Standard 1). This collaborative 
approach promotes shared ownership of both the project and the outcomes, fostering trust and 
transparency (WHO, 2020). 
 
Proactive Risk Assessment and Precautionary Planning 
In alignment with the precautionary principle (Rio Declaration, 1992), we conduct risk 
assessments that consider both scientifically substantiated risks and potential risks for which 
conclusive evidence may be lacking. This forward-looking strategy prioritises preventive action, 
ensuring that we address potential threats to community well-being before they materialise 
(IPBES, 2019). This includes designing strategies to minimise emissions, control waste, and limit 
noise, as well as implementing spill prevention protocols to protect water quality and prevent 
contamination (IFC Performance Standard 4). 
 
Monitoring and Responsive Adaptation 
Based on our ongoing monitoring and insights gathered through team interactions with the 
community, no significant adverse effects have been recorded to date. However, we remain 
vigilant. Monitoring systems are in place to identify early signs of potential impacts on community 
well-being or HCV attributes, allowing us to adapt our strategies as needed (HCV Resource 
Network). By prioritising community feedback, we ensure that adjustments are responsive to 
emerging issues or unforeseen challenges (IFC Performance Standard 1). 
 
Safety and Inclusivity Measures for Vulnerable Groups 
Specific measures to safeguard women, girls, children, and other marginalised groups are 
embedded in our project design (UNDP, 2018). For example, we implement safe worksite 
protocols (ILO, 1992), maintain accessible communication channels for reporting concerns, and 
promote training programmes on environmental safety and personal security (WHO, 2020). These 
proactive actions provide a secure environment and support community empowerment by 
equipping individuals with knowledge and resources to contribute to and benefit from the project 
sustainably. 
 
Alignment with the Precautionary Principle 
These measures exemplify our commitment to the precautionary principle, where we prioritise the 
prevention of harm even in the absence of complete scientific certainty (Rio Declaration, 1992). 
Our approach reflects the belief that safeguarding community well-being and protecting 
environmental attributes are foundational to achieving sustainable, long-term outcomes (IPBES, 
2019). This forward-thinking stance ensures that the health, safety, and rights of all community 
members remain central to our operational philosophy.

The project’s community-focused monitoring activities are closely aligned with four of the six 
implementation pillars: (1) Sustainable Livelihoods, (2) Community Resilience and Capacity 
Building, (3) Conservation and Restoration, and (4) Institutional Strengthening and Stakeholder 
Engagement. 
For instance, indicators that track household income diversification, participation in agroforestry 
or aquaculture, and improved access to Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) link directly to the 
TOC’s sustainable livelihoods pillar. Similarly, data collected on education, water access, health 
services, and sanitation improvements reflect progress under the resilience and capacity-building 
objectives. 
The monitoring of community participation in reforestation, fire prevention, and biodiversity 
conservation activities also reinforces the conservation pillar, especially with respect to 
maintaining and enhancing High Conservation Values (HCVs) related to ecosystem services, 
livelihood resources, and cultural identity. Finally, tracking participation in governance processes, 
legal empowerment programmes (e.g., social forestry), and FPIC sessions supports institutional 
strengthening and reflects the project’s commitment to inclusive and rights-based development. 
By embedding these indicators into a consistent and adaptive monitoring system, the project 
ensures that its Theory of Change is not just a planning tool, but a practical guide for 
implementation and impact evaluation throughout its 60-year lifespan. 
 
Alignment with Gold Level Criteria 
The monitoring plan also fulfills the requirements for attaining Gold Level validation under the 
CCB Standards, both for climate change adaptation benefits (GL1) and exceptional community 
benefits (GL2). 
To meet GL1, the plan includes specific indicators that capture communities’ adaptive capacity to 
climate-related risks. These include the use of sustainable livelihood strategies (such as 
agroforestry and diversified food systems), perceptions of climate vulnerability, and access to 
clean water and healthcare services—each of which contributes to enhanced community 
resilience in the face of environmental change. The project also monitors how communities 
participate in and benefit from rewetting, fire prevention, and habitat restoration activities—
measures that both reduce climate-related threats and build local adaptive knowledge. 
To comply with GL2, the project incorporates well-being and equity-focused indicators, with 
particular attention to women’s participation and empowerment. The monitoring plan captures 
gender-disaggregated data on training participation, income generation, leadership in community 
institutions, and access to education and health services. This approach ensures that the 
differentiated needs and contributions of women, youth, and marginalised groups are clearly 
understood and responded to over time. Community self-evaluation mechanisms, such as focus

Adaptive Management & Community Feedback 
Real-time data review, annual reflection workshops, and community self-evaluations ensure that

2.3.10 Stakeholder Participation in Decision-Making and Implementation (G3.6)

The Katingan Project has adopted a formal grievance and redress procedure to prevent and 
handle any conflicts with and among communities and other stakeholders which may arise 
during the implementation of project activities.

One of the most important elements of the grievance redress procedure is to prevent potential 
conflicts before they arise. Such precautionary approaches include the implementation of 
FPIC-based community consultations, participatory planning and regular communication. This 
helps to identify underlying grievances well in advance and allows them to be addressed. The 
formal village level planning processes also help to strengthen the bargaining position of 
project-zone communities when dealing with other stakeholders.

If any grievances occur and are reported from the project-zone communities and/or other 
relevant stakeholders in the form of letters, short messages or verbal communication, PT. 
RMU will quickly respond to them by following the formal handling process as shown in Figure

grievances, and PT. RMU’s verification team will recommend resolution options based on the 
feedback from the stakeholders. The degree of intervention and process will depend on the

The Katingan Project adopts FPIC principles in all community consultation processes (see

With the issuance of Ministry of Environment and Forestry no P70, P71, P72 and P73 in late 
December 2017, REDD projects within the jurisdiction of Indonesia should now be registered 
with the newly created National Registry System. It is also proposed that this may in turn 
make projects eligible to receive Result Based Payments for avoided emissions. However, 
this law is yet to be trialed, and it is currently unclear whether in future the Katingan Project 
will become eligible for such payments. Avoided carbon emission generated in this monitoring

providing input to their design and conducting a series of public consultations to test the 
standards at the Katingan Project site. This helped the Government of Indonesia integrate 
important safeguard standards in its national REDD+ policy framework development.

The project area stores vast amounts of CO2, and plays a vital role in stabilizing water flows,

This monitoring report covers the period from January 1st, 2018 through December 31st, 2019 in 
respect of CCB, and January 1st, 2019 through December 31st, 2019 in respect of VCS.  During 
this time, the project continued to build upon activities conducted during the first monitoring period 
and introduced new activities as required. Conservation and reforestation efforts focused on fire 
prevention and awareness training and seedling nursery development.  Community activities 
included ongoing support on community-based business development and community 
empowerment and development programs. Some business development activities such as 
microfinance, coconut sugar and sustainable agriculture remained our focus on this period, 
including the introduction of bamboo project, whereas other activities were shifted into other

CO2e, of which 130,873.81 were due to the continued decomposition from the 2015 fires. A small 
amount of deforestation occurred in 2019 (84.36 ha) which resulted in 29,532.52 CO2e  and 
105,418.71 CO2e were lost due to degradation, but losses in terms of emissions (against prior 
predictions) were small in comparison to the total number of credits generated.
